\begin{document}

\title{RT-IIPF: A Real-Time Inline Payment Fraud Mitigation
Framework Using Fused Isolation Forests and Local Outlier Factors}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{M. Parthasarathy}
\IEEEauthorblockA{\textit{Department of Computer Science and Engineering} \\
\textit{Sathyabama Institute of Science and Technology}\\
Chennai, India}
}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Instant payment networks settle irrevocably, so a control that scores a
transaction after commit acts on funds that have already moved. This
paper presents RT-IIPF, which evaluates a payment inside the database
transaction while both ledger rows are held under write locks and the
debit remains uncommitted; a fraudulent transfer is rolled back
atomically and never persists in the ledger. Scoring runs three tiers
over a $67$-dimensional vector: rules whose thresholds are training
quantiles, an Isolation Forest, and a Local Outlier Factor estimator
over a fixed $40{,}000$-point reference set. The learned tiers combine
as $0.2\,S_{\mathrm{IF}} + 0.8\,S_{\mathrm{LOF}}$, floored by rule risk
and thresholded at $\tau = 0.802$, fixed by a matched
false-positive-rate sweep at $\mathrm{FPR}=0.0086$. On $50{,}000$ clean
and $400$ injected transactions the deployed configuration attains
recall $0.745$, precision $0.380$, and F1 $0.503$. Account lockout
commits through an independent \texttt{REQUIRES\_NEW} transaction and
survives the ledger rollback. Inference costs $17.3$\,ms and end-to-end
switch latency is $22.4$\,ms at unit concurrency, with single-worker p95
within a $500$\,ms budget up to $25$ concurrent clients. Contended and
uncontended throughput are statistically indistinguishable, so the
system is not lock-bound. We report two negative results: the Isolation
Forest tier changes no verdict while consuming $55.1\%$ of inference
cost, and rule escalation reduces precision without increasing recall.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Payment systems, anomaly detection, isolation forest, local outlier
factor, real-time switches, transactional rollback.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Instant retail payment networks settle irrevocably. Once a Unified
Payments Interface (UPI) transfer commits, funds reach the beneficiary
within seconds and recovery depends on intermediary cooperation rather
than on reversal. The interval in which a payment can be stopped at
zero cost is the interval before the database transaction commits,
measured in milliseconds. Most deployed controls do not operate inside
it: they score after settlement, which converts a detection problem
into a recovery problem.

An inline control spends part of the switch's processing window, and
because it runs while both ledger rows sit under
\texttt{PESSIMISTIC\_WRITE} locks, it also extends the interval in
which those two accounts are unavailable to every other payment. The
cost is twofold: response latency and lock occupancy. We adopt a
$500$\,ms round-trip budget as the design
target.\footnote{This is the present work's engineering
budget; a citation to the governing network specification should
replace this note before submission.} The implementation reported here
spends $17.3$\,ms of inference inside a $22.4$\,ms path, and that
sub-$20$\,ms inference figure, not the $500$\,ms envelope, is the
constraint that excludes most published detectors.

Batch pipelines impose no latency on the authorisation path but act on
funds already moved. Sequential~\cite{jurgovsky2018} and
graph~\cite{dou2020} detectors read behavioural and relational context
that a single transaction record cannot carry, and in this setting they
pay for it twice: once in inference, and again in the database work
needed to assemble that history or neighbourhood while the payer's row
is already locked. Both are supervised, so they want labels that are
scarce precisely when a pattern is novel. What the authorisation path
needs instead is a detector that scores one record in isolation,
cheaply enough to fit inside the lock window, with no labels, no second
query, and a verdict the transaction manager can act on before commit.
This paper contributes:

\textbf{C1.} An inline hybrid pipeline combining a deterministic rule
tier with an Isolation Forest and a Local Outlier Factor estimator,
fused by a weighted blend that is floored by rule risk and thresholded
at $\tau=0.802$. The pipeline is stateless and deterministic, so
verdicts are reproducible during audit.

\textbf{C2.} A decoupled switch that preserves a security invariant
under rollback: on a fraud verdict the account lock and the audit
record commit through an independent \texttt{REQUIRES\_NEW} transaction
that completes \emph{before} the financial transaction rolls back, so
security state persists while the ledger is left arithmetically
unchanged.

\textbf{C3.} Measurement of the inline cost, including negative
results. Single-worker p95 stays within budget to $25$ concurrent
clients and exceeds it at $50$. The Isolation Forest tier changes no
verdict on our evaluation set, and rule escalation reduces precision
without increasing recall.

%%=====================================================================
\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:relatedwork}

\textbf{Rule engines} remain the default inline control for
architectural rather than statistical reasons: threshold conjunctions
evaluate in constant time, hold no model state, emit a reason code, and
fail reconstructibly. Surveys record them as the component that
executes on the authorisation path, with learned models placed
downstream~\cite{abdallah2016}. The limits are equally well known, and
each one shaped a decision here. A fixed predicate set encodes only the
attacks known when it was written, so we do not ask this tier to
classify. Absolute thresholds drift as the amount distribution moves,
so ours are training quantiles: $\theta_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is
\INR{16{,}450.01}, not a round \INR{16{,}000} chosen by hand. And a
conjunction over individual attributes cannot express an anomaly spread
\emph{across} attributes, so the tier supplies a lower bound on risk
and leaves that case to the density estimator.

\textbf{Supervised and deep models.} Gradient-boosted trees are the
standard tabular baseline~\cite{chen2016}; sequential~\cite{jurgovsky2018}
and graph~\cite{dou2020} architectures add behavioural and relational
context~\cite{adewumi2017}. Three properties of this family bear on
inline use, and they compound. Labels come first: a confirmed fraud
label takes days to weeks to produce, so the label set is empty exactly
when a novel pattern must be caught. Label \emph{quality} is the
second, and our corpus shows how badly it can fail --- the shipped
\texttt{fraud\_flag} column yields ROC-AUC $\approx 0.48$ against every
detector we evaluated, which is to say it carries no signal at all, and
any retraining loop built on it would optimise noise. The third applies
only to the sequential and graph variants, which must assemble a
history or a neighbourhood at scoring time and so add database work to
the very window they extend. The unsupervised per-transaction
formulation used here sidesteps all three. It pays for that in two
ways: it detects \emph{atypicality} rather than \emph{fraud}, and it is
blind to velocity attacks by construction, which we quantify with a
negative control rather than leave implicit.

\textbf{Unsupervised ensembles.} Isolation Forest~\cite{liu2008} scores
by expected path length under random axis-parallel splits, and its cost
does not grow with the training set --- the property that put it in
this pipeline to begin with. It weakens where anomalies are local
rather than globally extreme, and, as
Section~\ref{sec:evaluation} measures on our own $67$-dimensional
encoding, where $64$ of those coordinates are one-hot indicators with
only $10$ set in any record. Local Outlier
Factor~\cite{breunig2000} covers exactly that case through local
density contrast, and inverts the cost structure: each query scales
with the reference set, so scoring against the full $200{,}000$-row
training partition would have exhausted the lock window on its own.
One-class SVMs~\cite{scholkopf2001} run into the same wall. With no
method uniformly dominant~\cite{campos2016}, we combined rather than
chose, and capped the density term at a $40{,}000$-point reference set
drawn once and held resident --- $184$\,MB of the scoring process,
which is what fixes the worker count in
Section~\ref{sec:implementation}.

The closest prior work scores UPI records drawn from the same public
source~\cite{kumar2026}, but issues a step-up challenge \emph{after}
the model clears a transaction, in application flow, and reports no
latency. Its published confusion matrix ($\mathrm{TN}{=}75$,
$\mathrm{FP}{=}6$, $\mathrm{FN}{=}85$, $\mathrm{TP}{=}14$) implies
accuracy $49.4\%$ and recall $14.1\%$, which disagrees with the
accuracy stated in the same paper. We therefore avoid accuracy
entirely: at our $0.79\%$ prevalence, a detector that flags nothing
scores $99.21\%$.

%%=====================================================================
\section{Hybrid Inference Pipeline}
\label{sec:methodology}

\subsection{Data Ingestion and Feature Vectorisation}

A payment is described by $13$ components: three numeric (amount, hour
of day, weekend flag) and ten categorical (transaction type, merchant
category, sender and receiver age group, sender state, sender and
receiver bank, device type, network type, day of week). These arrive
from three distinct sources, shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:ingest}. The payer
supplies three through the form. The client runtime contributes two as
background telemetry, read from the browser rather than typed. The
switch resolves the remaining eight from its own account records and
its clock, at the moment the ledger rows are locked. Nothing is taken
from the payee, and nothing depends on the outcome being scored, so the
vector is complete before any money moves.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=2.2mm and 3.4mm]
\node[fbox, text width=0.29\columnwidth] (f1)
  {\textbf{Payer form}\\ amount, type,\\ merchant category\\ \emph{(3 fields)}};
\node[fbox, text width=0.29\columnwidth, right=of f1] (f2)
  {\textbf{Client runtime}\\ device type,\\ network type\\ \emph{(2 fields)}};
\node[fbox, text width=0.29\columnwidth, right=of f2] (f3)
  {\textbf{Switch + clock}\\ banks, age groups,\\ state, hour, day\\ \emph{(8 fields)}};
\node[shaded, below=5.5mm of f2, text width=0.80\columnwidth, align=center] (pre)
  {\textbf{Preprocessor $\Phi$} \emph{(fitted once, seed 42)}\\[1pt]
   3 numeric standardised $\;\cdot\;$ 10 categorical one-hot
   $\rightarrow$ 64\\ unseen levels $\rightarrow$ all-zero block};
\node[heavy, below=3.6mm of pre, text width=0.80\columnwidth, align=center] (vec)
  {$\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{67}$ \quad ($3$ dense $+$ $64$ binary,
   exactly $10$ non-zero)};
\foreach \s in {f1,f2,f3} \draw[flow] (\s) -- (pre);
\draw[flow] (pre) -- (vec);
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Ingestion and vectorisation. Thirteen raw components from
three sources embed into $d=67$ coordinates. The sparsity of the
one-hot block, $10$ non-zero of $64$, is what separates the two learned
tiers in Section~\ref{sec:evaluation}.}
\label{fig:ingest}
\end{figure}

Both learned tiers share the embedding $\Phi$, fitted once on the
training partition. Numeric components are standardised; categorical
components are one-hot expanded, and an unseen level encodes to an
all-zero block so the service remains total over arbitrary input rather
than raising on a value absent from training. The one-hot blocks
contribute $64$ coordinates, giving $d = 3 + 64 = 67$, of which $64$
are binary and exactly $10$ are non-zero in any record. This geometry
is not incidental presentation detail: it governs the relative
performance of the two learned tiers, and
Section~\ref{sec:evaluation} returns to it. Training uses $200{,}000$
rows, an $80\%$ split of a $250{,}000$-row corpus under seed~$42$.

\subsection{Three Tiers over One Vector}

\textbf{Tier 1, rules.} Four predicates evaluate directly on the raw
fields. Their thresholds are quantiles of the training amount
distribution rather than authored round numbers: the extreme threshold
is the $99.9$th percentile, \INR{16{,}450.01}; the high threshold is
the $99.0$th percentile, \INR{8{,}998.01}; and the small-ticket ceiling
is the $99.5$th percentile, \INR{11{,}136.03}. The predicates are an extreme
amount (weight $0.55$); a high amount in the small hours, at or before
$05$:$00$ (weight $0.30$); a small-ticket category such as Grocery,
Food, Transport or a Recharge exceeding the small-ticket ceiling
(weight $0.35$); and a high amount originating from the Web channel
rather than a mobile application (weight $0.20$). The weights sum
into a clipped rule risk $R \in [0,1]$. A separate hard flag $H$ fires
either when the extreme predicate alone is satisfied, or when any two
predicates are satisfied together. The flag encodes two distinct
arguments for blocking: one predicate strong enough on its own, or
corroboration across independent predicates.

\textbf{Tier 2, Isolation Forest.} We fit $200$ isolation trees with
subsample size $256$ and contamination $0.002$ on the embedded
training partition. The tree ensemble scores a record by how short a
path of random axis-parallel splits isolates it. The raw score is
mapped onto $[0,1]$ by a linear calibration whose lower anchor is the
training minimum and whose upper anchor is the $99.95$th percentile
rather than the maximum, so that a single extreme training point
cannot compress the usable range.

\textbf{Tier 3, Local Outlier Factor.} We draw $40{,}000$ points
uniformly without replacement from the embedded training partition and
fit a novelty-mode estimator with $k=20$ neighbours under the Euclidean
metric. The estimator compares the local density around a query point
against the density around its neighbours; values above unity indicate
a locally sparse neighbourhood. The same percentile calibration maps
the result onto $[0,1]$. Fixing the reference set is what makes this
tier admissible inline: query cost is bounded by a constant chosen at
training time rather than growing with the corpus.

\subsection{Fusion and Decision}

The two learned scores combine convexly, with weights fixed by a sweep
on the injected evaluation set, and the rule tier enters as a
\emph{floor} rather than as a third addend:
\begin{equation}
S = \max\big\{\,0.2\,S_{\mathrm{IF}} + 0.8\,S_{\mathrm{LOF}},\;\;
R \,\big\} .
\label{eq:fused}
\end{equation}
The choice of $\max$ over a three-way weighted sum is deliberate. It
guarantees $S \geq R$ at every point, so no combination of learned
scores can place a transaction below the risk the rules assign it. A
weighted sum would permit exactly that cancellation, letting two
confident low learned scores dilute a fired rule. The verdict is then
\begin{equation}
\hat{y} = \mathbb{1}\!\left[\, S \geq \tau \;\;\vee\;\; H \,\right],
\qquad \tau = 0.802 ,
\label{eq:decide}
\end{equation}
with $\tau$ fixed by the matched false-positive-rate sweep of
Section~\ref{sec:evaluation} and serialised into the model bundle, so
the deployed boundary is the evaluated one. The disjunction is not
redundant, and Section~\ref{subsec:sweep} exhibits a transaction that
blocks through $H$ at $S = 0.550 < \tau$.

Equation~\eqref{eq:decide} involves no randomness, no dependence on
request order, and no mutable state. The detectors are loaded once at
startup and are read-only thereafter. Identical inputs therefore yield
identical verdicts across processes and restarts, which is what an
audit of a declined payment requires.

%%=====================================================================
\section{Inline Transaction Switch}
\label{sec:architecture}

\subsection{Decoupled Topology}

Fig.~\ref{fig:arch} shows the split. A Java~21 / Spring~Boot switch
owns authentication, ledger state, locks, and the commit decision,
embedding an H2 engine in-process so that no network hop separates the
application from its own locks. A containerised Python / FastAPI node
owns inference, holding the preprocessor, both detectors, and the
$40{,}000 \times 67$ reference matrix resident in memory. The scoring
node is stateless: it performs no writes and joins no distributed
transaction, so it cannot corrupt ledger state under any failure mode.
Its worst possible contribution is unavailability, and
Section~\ref{subsec:failclosed} defines what the switch does with that.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node[shaded, text width=0.345\columnwidth] (sw)
  {\textbf{Spring Boot Switch}\\ \emph{Java 21, authoritative}\\[2pt]
   $\cdot$ MPIN auth, lock check\\
   $\cdot$ H2 \textbf{in-process}\\
   $\cdot$ \texttt{PESSIMISTIC}\\
   \quad \texttt{\_WRITE}, ascending\\
   \quad user id\\
   $\cdot$ $T_{f}$: debit $+$ credit\\
   $\cdot$ $T_{s}$: \texttt{REQUIRES}\\
   \quad \texttt{\_NEW} lock $+$ audit};
\node[shaded, text width=0.345\columnwidth, right=19mm of sw] (ml)
  {\textbf{FastAPI Inference}\\ \emph{stateless, read-only}\\[2pt]
   $\cdot$ uvicorn, $W{=}1$\\
   $\cdot$ bundle $184$\,MB RSS\\
   $\cdot$ $\Phi \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{67}$\\
   $\cdot$ IF: $200$ trees\\
   $\cdot$ LOF: $k{=}20$ over\\
   \quad $40{,}000 \times 67$\\
   \quad resident matrix\\
   $\cdot$ $512$\,MB container};
\draw[flow] ($(sw.east)+(0,5mm)$) -- node[above, font=\tiny, align=center,
  inner sep=1.5pt] {\texttt{POST}\\ \texttt{/score}} ($(ml.west)+(0,5mm)$);
\draw[flow] ($(ml.west)+(0,-5mm)$) -- node[below, font=\tiny, align=center,
  inner sep=1.5pt] {$S$, $\hat{y}$,\\ reasons} ($(sw.east)+(0,-5mm)$);
\node[font=\tiny, align=center, below=2.4mm of sw, text width=0.40\columnwidth]
  {connect $300$\,ms, read $1500$\,ms:\\ timeouts bound lock hold};
\node[font=\tiny, align=center, below=2.4mm of ml, text width=0.40\columnwidth]
  {no writes, no 2PC:\\ cannot corrupt the ledger};
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Decoupled architecture. The switch holds all authority; the
scoring node holds all model state. The call is synchronous because an
asynchronous hop would place the verdict after the commit boundary.}
\label{fig:arch}
\end{figure}

The scoring hop is \emph{synchronous and blocking}, which is a
requirement rather than an implementation shortcut. The switch issues
the call from inside an open \texttt{@Transactional} method while
holding write locks on both balance rows, suspending the request thread
for the round trip. An asynchronous hop would place the verdict after
the commit boundary and so reduce the design to post-settlement
detection with extra latency. The switch guarantees that the lock
precedes the score and the score precedes the commit, for every
transaction that commits.

\subsection{Locking Discipline}

Both ledger rows are acquired under \texttt{PESSIMISTIC\_WRITE}, which
issues \texttt{SELECT \ldots{} FOR UPDATE}. Optimistic versioning is
unsuitable here because retry-on-conflict would re-invoke the scorer,
multiplying the dominant cost term on exactly the contended path where
latency matters most. Locks are taken in ascending user-identifier
order. That total order eliminates the cyclic wait-for condition, so
two opposing concurrent payments between the same pair of accounts
serialise rather than deadlock. The discipline is necessary, not
precautionary: each transaction holds its first lock across a network
round trip, which widens the window in which a cycle could form by
roughly three orders of magnitude over a pure database update.

\subsection{Execution Lifecycle and the Security Boundary}

Fig.~\ref{fig:lifecycle} traces a payment. Three terminal states
persist: \texttt{SUCCESS} commits both legs and returns HTTP~200;
\texttt{BLOCKED\_FRAUD} rolls back and locks the payer, returning
HTTP~403; and \texttt{FAILED} covers pre-verdict rejections and scorer
unavailability.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[
  node distance=2.0mm,
  step/.style={fbox, text width=0.78\columnwidth},
  lockd/.style={step, fill=black!6},
]
\node[step]  (n1) {\textbf{1}~Validate request, resolve payer, check
  account lock flag, verify MPIN};
\node[lockd, below=of n1] (n2) {\textbf{2}~\textsc{begin} $T_{f}$:
  lock both rows \texttt{FOR UPDATE}, ascending id};
\node[lockd, below=of n2] (n3) {\textbf{3}~Apply debit and credit ---
  \emph{uncommitted, visible to no one}};
\node[lockd, below=of n3] (n4) {\textbf{4}~Thread \textbf{suspends}
  $\rightarrow$ \texttt{/score} $\rightarrow$ $S_{\mathrm{IF}},
  S_{\mathrm{LOF}}, R \rightarrow \hat{y}$};
\node[heavy, below=of n4, text width=0.78\columnwidth] (n5)
  {\textbf{5}~If $\hat{y}{=}1$: open $T_{s}$
  (\texttt{REQUIRES\_NEW}, separate connection)\\
  $\rightarrow$ set lock flag $+$ insert audit row $\rightarrow$
  \textsc{commit} $T_{s}$ at $t_{1}$};
\node[step, below=of n5] (n6) {\textbf{6}~$\hat{y}{=}1$:
  \textsc{rollback} $T_{f}$ at $t_{2} > t_{1}$, HTTP 403
  ~\textbar~ $\hat{y}{=}0$: \textsc{commit} $T_{f}$, HTTP 200};
\foreach \a/\b in {n1/n2, n2/n3, n3/n4, n4/n5, n5/n6}
  \draw[flow] (\a) -- (\b);
\begin{scope}[on background layer]
  \node[draw, dashed, fit=(n2)(n3)(n4), inner sep=2.6pt] (win) {};
\end{scope}
\node[rotate=90, anchor=south, font=\tiny\itshape]
  at ($(win.west)+(-1.2mm,0)$) {rows locked};
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Execution lifecycle. Steps 2--4 hold both balance rows under
\texttt{PESSIMISTIC\_WRITE} across the scoring round trip. Step~5
commits on an independent connection and therefore survives the
rollback in step~6.}
\label{fig:lifecycle}
\end{figure}

A rollback that discards the fraudulent debit would, under a single
transaction, also discard the evidence of the attempt and the account
lock raised in response. The switch therefore separates the two. Let
$T_{f}$ be the financial transaction and $T_{s}$ a second transaction
declared \texttt{Propagation.REQUIRES\_NEW}. On a fraud verdict the
switch suspends $T_{f}$, opens $T_{s}$ on a separate connection, sets
the payer's lock flag, inserts the \texttt{BLOCKED\_FRAUD} audit row,
and commits $T_{s}$ at $t_{1}$; it then resumes $T_{f}$ and raises the
fraud exception, rolling back at $t_{2} > t_{1}$. Because $T_{s}$
commits strictly first and on an independent connection, the effects
satisfy
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{eff}(T_{s}) \neq \emptyset
\;\;\wedge\;\;
\mathrm{eff}(T_{f}) = \emptyset ,
\label{eq:invariant}
\end{equation}
so the lock and the audit record persist while both balances are left
arithmetically untouched. The ordering is not interchangeable:
committing $T_{s}$ after raising the exception would place the write on
an unwinding stack, and nesting it inside $T_{f}$ would discard it
along with the debit. We verified \eqref{eq:invariant} by observing the
audit row count increment across a rollback while both balances
retained their pre-transaction values.

%%=====================================================================
\section{Implementation Details}
\label{sec:implementation}

\subsection{Fail-Closed Semantics}
\label{subsec:failclosed}

Every non-success outcome of the scoring call --- connection refused,
read timeout, malformed response, non-2xx status --- raises a single
scoring-unavailable fault that yields HTTP~503 and a rollback. No code
path commits an unscored payment. The alternative is directly
exploitable: a system that admits payments when its scorer is
unreachable can be opened by denying service to the scorer, which is
cheaper than defeating the detector. The policy has an operational
cost, and we state it rather than hide it. A cold container converts
the first request into a rejection, as Section~\ref{subsec:latency}
quantifies.

The two timeouts are not interchangeable settings. The connect timeout
is $300$\,ms and the read timeout $1500$\,ms. Because the call is
issued with both ledger rows locked, the read timeout is the hard
ceiling on lock-hold time, not merely a bound on request duration. It
is the parameter that keeps a slow scorer from becoming a ledger-wide
availability incident.

\subsection{Worker Count and the Container Budget}

The scoring node runs under uvicorn with \texttt{WEB\_CONCURRENCY=1}.
This is a measured constraint rather than a default. Each worker is a
separate OS process that loads its own copy of the model bundle,
measured at $184$\,MB resident, rising to $220$--$250$\,MB with the
server and interpreter. Against the $512$\,MB container limit of the
deployment target, two workers are the arithmetic maximum and leave no
headroom for the transient allocation of the $k$-neighbour query. We
therefore set one worker and accept the throughput ceiling that
Section~\ref{subsec:latency} measures, rather than risk an
out-of-memory kill that the fail-closed policy would turn into blanket
payment rejection.

The reference matrix is read-only after startup. No request mutates
shared state, so handlers are race-free without locking inside the
scorer, and a single worker loses no correctness guarantee relative to
several. Configuration is environment-driven throughout: service URLs,
CORS origins, and both timeouts are injected rather than compiled in,
so the laboratory and cloud deployments run byte-identical images.

\subsection{Reproducibility}

Seed~$42$ fixes the train/test split, the forest's randomisation, and
the reference-set draw. The calibration anchors, the four rule
thresholds, the fusion weights, and $\tau$ are all serialised into the
same bundle as the fitted estimators, so a redeployment cannot silently
change the decision boundary while appearing to load the same model.
The bundle records its own \texttt{scikit-learn} version, since the
estimators' internals are not guaranteed stable across releases.

%%=====================================================================
\section{Experimental Evaluation and Discussion}
\label{sec:evaluation}

\subsection{Setup and Ground Truth}

An $80/20$ split of the $250{,}000$-record corpus under seed~$42$
yields $200{,}000$ training rows and $50{,}000$ held-out clean rows. We
do not use the corpus's shipped \texttt{fraud\_flag} as ground truth:
it yields ROC-AUC $\approx 0.48$ against every detector we evaluated,
indistinguishable from random, so supervised metrics against it would
measure the label rather than the detector.

Instead we sample real clean held-out rows and overwrite only the
fields that define each archetype, leaving every other field at its
sampled value, so that synthetics are not separable by a generation
artefact. Four archetypes of $100$ instances give $400$ injected
transactions at $0.79\%$ prevalence: (A) off-hour drain,
\INR{25{,}000}--\INR{60{,}000} between $01$:$00$ and $04$:$00$ from
Web; (B) velocity spike, \INR{2{,}000}--\INR{6{,}000} in business hours
from Android; (C) category anomaly, \INR{50{,}000}--\INR{100{,}000} in
Grocery during daytime; and (D) context anomaly,
\INR{2{,}000}--\INR{9{,}000} before $05$:$00$ from Web over WiFi.

Archetype~B is a deliberate \emph{negative control}. Velocity is a
property of arrival rate, which no per-transaction vector carries, so
appreciable recall on~B would indicate leakage in the injection
procedure rather than detection. Sweeping $S$ to
$\mathrm{FPR} = 0.0086$ returns $\tau = 0.802$, and all comparisons
below are made at that matched false-positive rate so that no
configuration is advantaged by operating at a different point.

\subsection{Tier Ablation}
\label{subsec:ablation}

Fig.~\ref{fig:metrics} and Table~\ref{tab:ablation} report the
ablation. Three findings follow, two of them negative.

\emph{The density tier carries detection.} LOF alone raises recall from
$0.147$ to $0.745$ over the forest alone at identical false-positive
rate, a factor of $5.07$, and raises AUC from $0.7231$ to $0.8959$. The
cause is the geometry established in Section~\ref{sec:methodology}:
with $64$ of $67$ coordinates binary and only $10$ non-zero per record,
axis-parallel random splits fall predominantly on all-zero coordinates
and isolate almost nothing, whereas a density estimate reads the full
vector at once.

\emph{The forest contributes no detection.} Rows (c) and (d) of
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} agree to three decimals on precision, recall
and F1, and their per-archetype recalls coincide exactly --- A~$1.00$,
B~$0.01$, C~$1.00$, D~$0.97$ --- against the forest's own $0.26$,
$0.00$, $0.07$ and $0.26$. Adding the forest at weight $0.20$ changes
no verdict while \emph{reducing} fused AUC from $0.8959$ to $0.8812$.
The reading is unambiguous: on one-hot-dominated payment features a
partition-based detector adds nothing to a density-based one, and
Section~\ref{subsec:latency} shows it adds that nothing at
$55.1\%$ of inference cost. The $0.20$ weight is not a small
contribution; it is no contribution.

\emph{Escalation costs precision without adding recall.} The deployed
configuration holds recall at $0.745$ while precision falls to $0.380$
and the false discovery rate rises to $0.620$. Escalation buys no
recall whatsoever and costs $0.029$ of precision, and we keep it
anyway. The reasons are real but lie outside what this evaluation set
can score: the tier stays valid beyond the training support, where both
calibrations clip at unity and stop discriminating; it emits the reason
code a declined payment has to be defended with; and it enforces the
amount-monotonicity that Section~\ref{subsec:sweep} shows the learned
tiers do not have. We state the price rather than bury it.

Archetype~B returns recall $0.01$, within noise of the expected zero,
which supports the injection procedure. Excluding~B, the detectable
population is $300$ instances, of which the deployed system identifies
$297$, or $99.0\%$ of the attainable ceiling; aggregate recall is
bounded above by $0.75$ by construction. We report the unadjusted
figure and state the bound.

\subsection{Walking the Amount Domain}
\label{subsec:sweep}

Table~\ref{tab:sweep} holds every feature constant --- a P2M Grocery
payment from a Web client over 4G at $18$:$00$ on a weekday --- and
varies only the amount. Reading it row by row exposes three properties
that neither the aggregate metrics nor the architecture description
reveals.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Amount sweep, all other features held constant (P2M, Grocery,
Web, 4G, hour~18, weekday). Amounts in INR.}
\label{tab:sweep}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.12}
\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rccccl@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Amount} & $S_{\mathrm{IF}}$ & $S_{\mathrm{LOF}}$ & $R$ & $S$ & \textbf{Verdict} \\
\midrule
$50$            & $0.467$ & $0.340$ & $0.00$ & $0.365$ & ALLOW \\
$1{,}000$       & $0.461$ & $0.357$ & $0.00$ & $0.377$ & ALLOW \\
$5{,}000$       & $0.531$ & $0.814$ & $0.00$ & $0.757$ & ALLOW \\
$8{,}998^{a}$   & $0.593$ & $0.568$ & $0.00$ & $0.573$ & ALLOW \\
$11{,}136^{b}$  & $0.617$ & $0.519$ & $0.20$ & $0.538$ & ALLOW \\
$16{,}450^{c}$  & $0.617$ & $0.474$ & $0.55$ & $0.550$ & \textbf{BLOCK} \\
$20{,}000$      & $0.617$ & $0.537$ & $1.00$ & $1.000$ & \textbf{BLOCK} \\
$50{,}000$      & $0.617$ & $1.000$ & $1.00$ & $1.000$ & \textbf{BLOCK} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\vspace{2pt}
{\footnotesize\raggedright
$^{a,b,c}$Sweep amounts are rounded to the rupee and so fall just
\emph{below} $\theta_{\mathrm{high}}$, $\theta_{\mathrm{tick}}$ and
$\theta_{\mathrm{ext}}$ respectively, none of which is a round number.
The corresponding predicate therefore does not fire on that row.\par}
\end{table}

First, \emph{the learned score is not monotone in amount}. The density
score reaches $0.814$ at \INR{5{,}000} and falls to $0.519$ at
\INR{11{,}136}, a transfer more than twice as large in an otherwise
identical context. This is correct behaviour for a density statistic:
\INR{5{,}000} happens to occupy a thinner region of the Grocery/P2M
population than \INR{11{,}136} does. But it means a policy requiring
that risk never decrease as the amount rises cannot be expressed by the
learned tiers at all. Column~$R$ is monotone by construction and
supplies precisely that guarantee, which is the strongest argument for
keeping a tier that Section~\ref{subsec:ablation} shows costs
precision.

Second, \emph{the decision disjunction is not redundant}. At
\INR{16{,}450} the system blocks with $S = 0.550$, well below
$\tau = 0.802$, so thresholding on the fused score alone would have
admitted this transaction. The verdict comes from the hard-flag branch
of \eqref{eq:decide}, and specifically from its corroboration clause
rather than from the extreme-amount predicate. Because the quantile
thresholds are not round numbers --- $\theta_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is
\INR{16{,}450.01} --- this row falls just under the extreme predicate,
which does not fire. Two weaker predicates fire instead, the
small-ticket category ceiling and the high-value Web channel, giving
$R = 0.35 + 0.20 = 0.55$ and satisfying $H$ through the two-predicate
clause. A rule tier that escalated only on a single dominant predicate
would have admitted this payment as well. The first transition in the
table therefore occurs between \INR{11{,}136} and \INR{16{,}450}, at
the rule boundary rather than at the learned boundary.

Third, the two endpoints are informative about what the model is
\emph{not} doing. The \INR{50} and \INR{50{,}000} rows share an
identical channel context --- same merchant category, device, network,
hour, and both counterparties --- and differ only in amount, yet
receive opposite verdicts, $S = 0.365$ against $S = 1.000$. The
boundary is driven by the transaction rather than by the channel: a
Web-origin Grocery payment is not rejected categorically, which a
coarser rule set would do and which would be unusable in production.

\subsection{Latency, Scaling and Lock Contention}
\label{subsec:latency}

Table~\ref{tab:components} decomposes inference on the laboratory host
over $n=300$ warm iterations. The ordering is the result that matters:
the forest consumes the largest single share, $55.1\%$, while
contributing no detection at all by
Section~\ref{subsec:ablation}. Dropping it would cut inference to about
$7.8$\,ms and change no verdict. We report the configuration we
actually deployed and measured, rather than the faster one we would
build next, and this is the single change we would make first.

At concurrency~$1$, where no queuing occurs, the switch completes a
payment in mean $22.4$\,ms (p95~$23.8$, p99~$25.3$), attributing
roughly $5.1$\,ms to switch-side work: MPIN verification, lock
acquisition, JPA flush, and HTTP serialisation in both directions. The
lock-hold window spans steps 2--4 of Fig.~\ref{fig:lifecycle} and so
lies between $17.3$\,ms and $22.4$\,ms, with a hard ceiling of
$1500$\,ms from the read timeout. That window is what the architecture
trades for pre-commit interception.

Fig.~\ref{fig:latency} places the laboratory figures against the cloud
deployment. On a $512$\,MB shared-CPU container, warm scorer-internal
inference measures mean $178.1$\,ms over $n=9$ samples, range
$101.4$--$235.1$\,ms, approximately $10\times$ the laboratory total.
The gap is attributable to CPU provisioning, not to the algorithm or to
HTTP transport, since the component ordering is unchanged. Observed
end-to-end switch latencies on the deployed instance were $337$\,ms and
$410$\,ms; a larger sample is required before reporting percentiles. A
single cold-start observation of $13{,}298$\,ms was recorded as the
first request after container idle eviction. It measures platform
container startup plus the roughly $1.8$\,s bundle load, and is
reported rather than discarded because the fail-closed policy of
Section~\ref{subsec:failclosed} converts a cold start into an HTTP~$503$
rejection, which is a real deployment consideration for platforms that
evict idle containers.

Table~\ref{tab:contention} compares an uncontended workload, in which
each virtual client holds a distinct account pair, against a contended
one in which all clients compete for an overlapping account set. Every
ratio equals or exceeds unity, so forcing all clients onto the same
ledger rows produced no measurable throughput penalty: the system is
not lock-bound. The binding constraint is the single-worker scorer,
which plateaus near $50$\,TPS and saturates before lock queuing becomes
observable. The ordering discipline of
Section~\ref{sec:architecture} held throughout, and no deadlock
occurred across the full benchmark.

Measured p95 stays within the $500$\,ms budget up to $25$ concurrent
clients ($374.5$\,ms) and exceeds it at $50$ ($864.2$\,ms), which
bounds the operating envelope of a single-worker deployment. A tail
effect appears at concurrency~$\geq 10$: p99 reaches $3.9$--$4.0$\,s in
\emph{both} workloads while p95 remains below $65$\,ms at
concurrency~$10$. Its equal magnitude under both conditions indicates
client-side connection queuing against the saturated scorer rather than
lock waiting, which is why Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} directs the
transport work at that number rather than at the locking discipline.

%%=====================================================================
\section{Conclusion and Future Work}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We implemented and measured a fraud control that executes inside the
database transaction, while ledger rows are locked and the debit is
uncommitted. A fraudulent transfer is rolled back atomically and never
persists, while the account lock and the audit record commit
independently and survive that rollback, the invariant
\eqref{eq:invariant} verified experimentally. The inline cost is
$17.3$\,ms of inference within a $22.4$\,ms path at unit concurrency,
and a lock window between those two figures.

The division of labour is not the one the design anticipated. Detection
is carried entirely by the density estimator: LOF alone matches the
fused configuration to three decimals, while the forest changes no
verdict at $55.1\%$ of inference cost. The rule tier buys bounds rather
than recall. It costs precision, $0.409$ falling to $0.380$, but
remains valid beyond the training support, emits the reason codes an
audit of a declined payment needs, and enforces the
amount-monotonicity the learned tiers demonstrably lack --- binding at
the \INR{16{,}450} point where the system blocks at $S = 0.550 < \tau$
on two corroborating predicates, neither individually decisive.
The system is not lock-bound; the scorer is the constraint.

Limitations bound these claims. The feature vector is
per-transaction, so velocity attacks are undetectable by construction,
as archetype~B's recall of $0.01$ confirms. Ground truth is synthetic,
the corpus labels being uninformative. The LOF calibration anchors are
computed in-sample on the reference set. The embedded database
preserves the audit trail for the process lifetime only. And the
results derive from one corpus and one geography.

Four directions follow. Multiplexed gRPC over Protocol Buffers targets
the $3.9$--$4.0$\,s p99, which the contention experiment identifies as
connection queuing rather than lock waiting, by removing connection
establishment, head-of-line blocking, and JSON serialisation from a
path that holds locks throughout. The reference set is frozen at
training time, so the density estimate ages under drift while its fixed
size bounds query cost; approximate nearest-neighbour indexing and a
rolling sharded reference set both apply, and both raise consistency
questions between replicas holding different reference states, since
\eqref{eq:decide} requires reproducible verdicts. Persisting the device
signature the client already captures but the model never receives
would admit an \texttt{is\_new\_device} feature addressing the
social-engineering case. Finally, routing scores just below $\tau$ to
out-of-band re-authentication would convert part of the $0.620$ false
discovery rate into a challenge rather than a block.
